steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on jailbreaks / prompt injection attacks against large language models. It should motivate the problem, walk through the actors in an attack using our Fig. 2 example, point out that formal study is missing, and summarize what we contribute.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs and the "pre-train, prompt, and predict" paradigm; new vulnerabilities
- Actors in a prompt injection attack (Fig. 2 example)
- Gap: little formal study of jailbreaks
- Our approach and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs and the prompting paradigm
  - Transformer-based generative LLMs: strong zero-/few-shot generalization (cite)
  - "pre-train, prompt, and predict": user gives task description + zero or more examples in natural language
  - instruction ("prompt") -> LLM performs new task on unseen examples
  - same ability exposes new vulnerabilities: "prompt injection attacks" / "jailbreaks"
  - point to Fig. 2 for example setup + actors

- Actors (Fig. 2)
  - application developers: use an LLM to build an application; here a translator, prompt model with translation task
  - end-users, two categories: benign (intended use case) vs malicious (tries to change model's goal via malicious input)
  - model outputs "Haha pwned!!" instead of translating
  - real-world attack on GPT-3 by a real user
  - user explorations -> avalanche of behavioral test-cases (cite)
  - intents: goal hijacking (failing the task), offensive/racist text, releasing private proprietary information
  - danger for content policy and regulations

- Gap
  - new jailbreak methods every day, but little formal study
  - missing: holistic picture of types/dimensions of attacks, severity, model vulnerability
  - existing studies limited, divergent; urgent need to consolidate (cite)

- Our approach / contributions
  - inspiration from other CS fields: computer security, SQL injection attacks
  - formalism of a "jailbreak"/"prompt-injection" + experimental setup to test claims
  - taxonomy of jailbreak characteristics
  - 3700 jailbreak prompts, templated approach
  - analysis of efficacy on different language models
  - attack detection tests (did the jailbreak succeed?)
  - code and data released (URL)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) that are generative and based on Transformers have shown very strong zero-shot and few-shot generalization under the new paradigm of "pre-train, prompt, and predict". In this paradigm any user can give a pretrained LLM a description of a task, followed by zero or more examples, all in natural language. Based on this instruction (which is called a "prompt"), the LLM can learn to do a new task on examples it has not seen. This ability to do a new task by following a natural language instruction is amazing, but it has also exposed a new set of vulnerabilities, which are popularly called "prompt injection attacks" or "jailbreaks". Fig. 2 shows an example of a prompt injection attack setup and the actors involved.

There are two types of actors in the pipeline in Fig. 2. The first type is the application developers, who use an LLM to build an application. In our example the developers want to build a translator, so they prompt the model with a translation task. The second type is the end-users, and they are divided into two categories. The first one is benign and uses the model for what it is intended for. The second user is malicious and tries to change the goal of the model by giving a malicious input. In the example the language model responds with "Haha pwned!!" and does not actually translate the sentence. The figure shows a real-world attack that was done on GPT-3 by a real user. These first explorations by users created an avalanche of such behavioral test-cases. Users showed that prompts can be designed with many intents, from goal hijacking (where the model just fails to do the task) to generating offensive, racist text, or even releasing private proprietary information. These attacks could also be dangerous for content policy and regulations.

- Gap
  - new jailbreak methods every day, but little formal study
  - missing: holistic picture of types/dimensions of attacks, severity, model vulnerability
  - existing studies limited, divergent; urgent need to consolidate (cite)

- Our approach / contributions
  - inspiration from other CS fields: computer security, SQL injection attacks
  - formalism of a "jailbreak"/"prompt-injection" + experimental setup to test claims
  - taxonomy of jailbreak characteristics
  - 3700 jailbreak prompts, templated approach
  - analysis of efficacy on different language models
  - attack detection tests (did the jailbreak succeed?)
  - code and data released (URL)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) that are generative and based on Transformers have shown very strong zero-shot and few-shot generalization under the new paradigm of "pre-train, prompt, and predict". In this paradigm any user can give a pretrained LLM a description of a task, followed by zero or more examples, all in natural language. Based on this instruction (which is called a "prompt"), the LLM can learn to do a new task on examples it has not seen. This ability to do a new task by following a natural language instruction is amazing, but it has also exposed a new set of vulnerabilities, which are popularly called "prompt injection attacks" or "jailbreaks". Fig. 2 shows an example of a prompt injection attack setup and the actors involved.

There are two types of actors in the pipeline in Fig. 2. The first type is the application developers, who use an LLM to build an application. In our example the developers want to build a translator, so they prompt the model with a translation task. The second type is the end-users, and they are divided into two categories. The first one is benign and uses the model for what it is intended for. The second user is malicious and tries to change the goal of the model by giving a malicious input. In the example the language model responds with "Haha pwned!!" and does not actually translate the sentence. The figure shows a real-world attack that was done on GPT-3 by a real user. These first explorations by users created an avalanche of such behavioral test-cases. Users showed that prompts can be designed with many intents, from goal hijacking (where the model just fails to do the task) to generating offensive, racist text, or even releasing private proprietary information. These attacks could also be dangerous for content policy and regulations.

New methods of jailbreaks come up every day, but so far there is little formal study of prompt injection attacks that gives a holistic idea of the types and dimensions of the attacks, how severe they are, and how vulnerable models are to them. The studies that exist are limited and divergent, and there is an urgent need to consolidate them.

We take inspiration from other fields of Computer Science where similar attacks have been studied, for example computer security and SQL injection attacks. Our approach to the problem is to present a formalism of a "jailbreak" or "prompt-injection", with an experimental setup to test our claims. We curate a taxonomy of the possible characteristics of jailbreaks, we provide 3700 jailbreak prompts that we made through a templated approach, and we give an analysis of how effective jailbreaks are on different language models. We also discuss attack detection tests to detect if a jailbreak was successful. Our code and data are available in this URL.

We take inspiration from other fields of Computer Science where similar attacks have been studied, for example computer security and SQL injection attacks. References:
[1] Kojima et al. (2022) Takeshi Kojima, Shixiang Shane Gu, Machel Reid, Yutaka Matsuo, and Yusuke Iwasawa. 2022. Large language models are zero-shot reasoners .
[2] Huang et al. (2022b) Wenlong Huang, Pieter Abbeel, Deepak Pathak, and Igor Mordatch. 2022b. Language models as zero-shot planners: Extracting actionable knowledge for embodied agents . In ICML 2022 , volume 162 of Proceedings of Machine Learning Research , pages 9118–9147. PMLR.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Transformers-based generative Large Language Models (LLM) have demonstrated superior zero-shot (and few-shot) generalization capabilities [1,2] under the new "pre-train, prompt, and predict" paradigm. In this paradigm, any user can provide a description of the task followed by zero or more examples in natural language to a pretrained LLM. Based on such an instruction (or "prompt"), the LLM can learn to perform a new task on unseen examples. This amazing ability to perform a new task by following a natural language instruction has also exposed a new set of vulnerabilities, popularly categorized as "prompt injection attacks" or "jailbreaks". Fig. 2 shows an example of a prompt injection attack setup and the associated actors.

In Fig. 2, we consider two types of actors in the pipeline. First are the application developers who use an LLM to build an application. In our example, the application developers aim to build a translator and prompt the model with a translation task. Then there are the end-users, who are divided into two categories. The first is benign, using the model for its intended use case. The second user maliciously attempts to change the model's goal by giving a malicious input. In this example, the language model responds with "Haha pwned!!" instead of actually translating the sentence. The figure depicts a real-world attack carried out on GPT-3 by a real user. These initial user-driven explorations created an avalanche of such behavioral test-cases [3]. Users demonstrated that prompts can be designed with intents ranging from goal hijacking (simply failing to perform the task) to generating offensive, racist text, or even releasing private proprietary information. Such attacks could also prove dangerous with respect to content policy and regulations.

While new methods of jailbreaks come up every day, to date there is little formal study of prompt injection attacks that portrays a holistic idea of the types and dimensions of attacks, their severity, and the vulnerability of models towards them. The existing studies [4,5] are limited and divergent, and there is an urgent need to consolidate them. Here, we draw inspiration from other fields of Computer Science (such as computer security and SQL injection attacks) where similar attacks have been studied. We approach this problem by presenting a formalism of a "jailbreak" or a "prompt-injection" along with an experimental setup to test our claims. We curate a taxonomy of the possible characteristics of jailbreaks, provide 3700 jailbreak prompts through a templated approach, and analyze the efficacy of jailbreaks on different language models. Additionally, we discuss attack detection tests to detect whether a jailbreak succeeded. Our code and data are available at this URL.

References:
[1] Kojima et al. (2022) Takeshi Kojima, Shixiang Shane Gu, Machel Reid, Yutaka Matsuo, and Yusuke Iwasawa. 2022. Large language models are zero-shot reasoners .
[2] Huang et al. (2022b) Wenlong Huang, Pieter Abbeel, Deepak Pathak, and Igor Mordatch. 2022b. Language models as zero-shot planners: Extracting actionable knowledge for embodied agents . In ICML 2022 , volume 162 of Proceedings of Machine Learning Research , pages 9118–9147. PMLR.
[3] Willison (2022) Simon Willison. 2022. Prompt injection .
[4] Kang et al. (2023) Daniel Kang, Xuechen Li, Ion Stoica, Carlos Guestrin, Matei Zaharia, and Tatsunori Hashimoto. 2023. Exploiting programmatic behavior of llms: Dual-use through standard security attacks .
[5] Greshake et al. (2023) Kai Greshake, Sahar Abdelnabi, Shailesh Mishra, Christoph Endres, Thorsten Holz, and Mario Fritz. 2023. More than you’ve asked for: A comprehensive analysis of novel prompt injection threats to application-integrated large language models .
